description: Hello! We are a team from Manaus, Amazonas, Brazil. We hold degrees in Computer Science Education.
summary: Amazon Fire is an open-source web app that harmonizes NASA MODIS and VIIRS hot spots into one consistent fire record from 2000 to 2026. The sensors count fire very differently (VIIRS sees two to three times more), and Suomi NPP, the VIIRS reference, stopped in November 2026. We calibrate each satellite hand-off month by month and test it on years the model never saw: the main MODIS and NOAA-20 hand-offs err by only 2–8% per year. With this record, anyone can pick any area of Brazil, by region, drawing or coordinates, and see when the burning season starts and peaks, where fire returns year after year, and how this year compares with the past. It matters because national averages hide local crises: in 2026 Brazil had its quietest fire season since 2001, while smoke-covered Manaus had its third most intense. The tool helps civil defense, firefighters, health services, land managers and scientists prepare before the smoke arrives.
details:
The problem

In the Amazon rainforest, fire rarely starts on its own. Lightning causes only 0.2–0.4% of the fires recorded each year in the Brazilian Amazon (Zhang et al., 2026); nearly all the rest are lit by people, to burn forest felled for deforestation or to renew pasture and fallow fields, and part of that fire escapes into the forest understory (Barlow et al., 2020). Drought makes all of them worse. During the 2015 drought, fire incidence in the Brazilian Amazon rose by 36% compared with the preceding 12 years, despite a 76% fall in deforestation rates (Aragão et al., 2018). The smoke is a public health problem across the region: preventing vegetation fires would avoid about 16,800 premature deaths in South America in a typical year (Butt et al., 2020), and deforestation fires alone had large air quality and health impacts in 2019 (Butt et al., 2021).

Manaus, the largest city in the Amazon, has lived through three smoke crises in four years (Table 1). In 2023 the Rio Negro reached its lowest level since 1902 and fine particulate matter (PM2.5) in the city reached 314.99 µg/m³, against a World Health Organization guideline of 15 µg/m³ (Ferrante et al., 2025). A study combining satellite data, air quality sensors and field visits identified the municipalities of Manaquiri, Careiro and Autazes, along the BR-319 and AM-254 highways, as the main sources of that smoke (Ferrante et al., 2025). In 2026 the state of Amazonas recorded 3,726 hotspots in September, 295.5% more than a year earlier, banned the use of fire for 120 days and declared an emergency in 36 municipalities (MPF, 2026).

Table 1. Recent smoke crises around Manaus

The people who prepare for these crises (civil defense, fire brigades, health services and environmental enforcement) need three answers: when the burning season starts, how the current year compares with the past, and where fire keeps coming back. NASA satellites can answer all three, because the Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) distributes every active fire detection since November 2000 (NASA FIRMS, 2026). The difficulty is that the record is not one record. MODIS has flown on Terra since 2000 and on Aqua since mid-2002, with 1 km pixels (Giglio et al., 2016). VIIRS has flown on Suomi NPP since 2012 and on NOAA-20 since 2018; its 375 m product responds to much smaller fires (Schroeder et al., 2014). Joined as they come, the counts show a fivefold jump in 2012 that is a change of sensor, not a change in fire (Fig. 1). A second break came on 2 November 2026, when NOAA ended delivery of all Suomi NPP products (NOAA NESDIS, 2026). Before August 2002 only Terra observed, in the morning, when fewer fires burn.

This project makes three contributions. First, it harmonizes the full FIRMS record into one series and measures the error of every satellite hand-off on held-out years. Second, it turns that series into a burn calendar for the Manaus metropolitan area: the typical season in dates, the 2026 season against it, and the places where fire recurs. Third, it applies the same method to all of Brazil and shows that a national calendar can point in the opposite direction from a local one, which is why the tool computes the calendar for any area its user chooses.

Fig. 1. Annual fire cell-days in the Manaus metropolitan area, 2001–2025. Grey dashed line: raw counts joined as they come (MODIS to 2011, VIIRS from 2012). Blue: harmonized series on the Suomi NPP scale.

Data and methods

Data

All fire detections come from NASA FIRMS (NASA FIRMS, 2026), archive and near real-time files, from 1 November 2000 to 14 November 2026 (Table 2). A first request covered the central Amazon (62–57.5°W, 5–1.5°S) and returned 365,885 detections. Unless stated otherwise, results for Manaus refer to the metropolitan box from 60.95°W to 58.90°W and 3.95°S to 2.55°S, which contains 151,618 detections after quality filtering. A second request covered all of Brazil and returned 41.6 million detections (about 3.4 GB). True-color images of the worst days come from NASA Worldview (NASA Worldview, 2026).

Table 2. Data used

Quality filter and common unit

We keep MODIS detections with confidence of 30 or more (Giglio et al., 2021) and VIIRS detections with nominal or high confidence (Schroeder et al., 2014), and only vegetation fires (type 0). Near real-time files, which cover the latest months, do not include the type field; there, any grid cell where the archive marks at least three non-vegetation detections, plus its eight neighbours, is treated as a fixed heat source. This removed 497 detections at 141 sources.

To make counts from different resolutions comparable, each detection is placed on a regular 0.01° grid (about 1.1 km) and counted at most once per cell, per day and per satellite. We call this unit a fire cell-day. It removes most of the advantage VIIRS has of producing several 375 m pixels for a single fire. Figure 2 summarizes the whole workflow.

Fig. 2. Method overview. (a) Operating periods of the four satellites and the three hand-offs calibrated in this study (H1–H3); Suomi NPP is the reference scale. (b) Processing chain from FIRMS detections to the burn calendar.

Calibrating the satellite hand-offs

For each calendar month m, the ratio between the reference series and the source series is computed over all months in which both observe, and shrunk toward the overall ratio R so that months with few fires remain stable:

R_m = (Σ reference_m + k·R) / (Σ source_m + k), k = 30

Three hand-offs are calibrated (Table 3). The harmonized series H equals Suomi NPP fire cell-days while Suomi NPP observes, NOAA-20 cell-days times Rm after it stopped, and MODIS cell-days times Rm before it started. The same ratios are applied day by day to build the daily calendar.

Table 3. Satellite hand-offs, Manaus metropolitan area

Validation

A calibration that fits only the data it was built on proves little. We use leave-one-year-out validation: each complete year of overlap is removed, the monthly ratios are recalibrated on the remaining years, and the removed year is predicted from the other sensor and compared with what Suomi NPP actually observed.

Typical year, season dates and recurrence

The typical year is the median, with the 25th and 75th percentiles, of the complete years 2003–2025, which excludes the Terra-only months. Daily harmonized counts are smoothed with a centered 15-day mean. The season starts on the first day the typical curve exceeds a quarter of its peak and ends on the last such day; the same rule dates each individual year. For the recurrence map, detections are also aggregated on a 0.04° grid (about 4.4 km), and for each square we count the number of years, out of 26, with at least one detection.

National extension

For Brazil, the same filter, unit and hand-offs are applied, and the ratios are calibrated on national totals. Results are stored on 0.5° squares (about 55 km). When a user selects an area, the application recalibrates the ratios for that area alone and repeats the held-out-year test, so every local result is reported with its own error. Macro-regions are built from these squares and approximate the official borders.

Results

Validation

Table 4 and Fig. 3 show the held-out tests. All 13 MODIS test years around Manaus are predicted within 17%. The largest error is in 2025 (−16.9%), the quietest year, where small absolute differences weigh more; the two most extreme years, 2015 and 2023, are predicted within 8%. No year is biased in one direction: seven are underestimated and six overestimated. At national scale, with many more fires to average over, all three hand-offs are more precise, including the Terra-only correction, which is unreliable locally (41%) but usable for Brazil (7.7%). Months before August 2002 around Manaus are therefore flagged as low confidence and excluded from the typical year.

Table 4. Leave-one-year-out validation of each hand-off

Fig. 3. Observed Suomi NPP fire cell-days and predictions from MODIS (left) and NOAA-20 (right) for years held out of the calibration, Manaus metropolitan area

The daily burn calendar of Manaus

Figure 4 is the burn calendar: one row per year and one mark per day since 2001. The burning season repeats every year as a band from late July to early December. The most intense years by August–October total are 2023, 2015, 2026 and 2009, all drought years; the quietest were 2008, 2025 and 2011. The typical season starts on 28 July, peaks on 24 October and ends on 2 December (Table 5). For planning, the early starts matter most: in eight of 23 years (2006, 2007, 2013, 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022 and 2023) the season began before 15 July, so preparation that starts in August arrives late in about one year in three.

Fig. 4. Daily burn calendar of the Manaus metropolitan area, 2001–2026. Harmonized fire detections per day; dotted lines mark the typical season start and end, and the blue box the 2026 burn ban up to 14 November.

Table 5. The burning season in dates, Manaus metropolitan area

The 2026 season

In 2026 the season started on 25 July, three days earlier than usual. Fire did not stop when the ban was declared on 9 September (Fig. 5). Activity kept rising and reached its maximum a month later, on 9 October, with fire in 535 cells of 1 km, the same day Manaus measured 344.5 µg/m³ of PM2.5 (MPF, 2026). It then dropped sharply in the second half of October. August to October totalled 5,394 fire cell-days, the third highest of 26 seasons, and the year up to 14 November reached 2.2 times a typical year. During the ban, from 9 September to 14 November, we counted 4,172 harmonized detections in the metropolitan area. Our data cannot tell whether the late-October drop came from enforcement, rain or both, but they give agencies a consistent baseline to evaluate it. From 1 to 14 November activity was back within the normal range (0.78 times a typical year).

Fig. 5. 2026 against the typical year, Manaus metropolitan area. Harmonized detections per day, 15-day mean; the shaded band is the middle half of years 2003–2025.

Where fire keeps coming back

Inside the metropolitan area, 662 squares of about 4 km burned in 15 or more of the 26 years, and several burned in every single year (Fig. 6). The most persistent clusters lie south and east of the Amazon and Solimões rivers, near Autazes, Careiro and Manaquiri, the same municipalities identified as the main PM2.5 sources in 2023 (Ferrante et al., 2025). Fire around Manaus is not random: it returns to the same places, which is where prevention and enforcement can have the most effect. The worst day of 2026 is visible from space as a grey haze south of the rivers (Fig. 7).

Fig. 6. 3D recurrence map from the application, October 2026. Column height: detections in the selected month. Color: number of years with fire, from 1 (light) to 20 or more (dark red). Numbered markers: the five places where fire repeats most, listed at left.

Fig. 7. Central Amazon on 9 October 2026, the worst day of the year. VIIRS NOAA-20 true color with that day’s detections in red. Source: NASA Worldview and FIRMS.

Brazil: a quiet year that hid a local crisis

Nationally, the typical season runs from 27 July to 2 December with a peak on 15 September, five weeks before the Manaus peak, because the Cerrado and the southern arc of deforestation burn earlier than the central Amazon. In 2026 the national season started on 15 August, 19 days late, and its worst day was also 9 October.

From August to October 2026 Brazil burned 0.51 times a typical year, its quietest season in 26 years (Table 6, Fig. 8). The Center-West, Southeast and South had their quietest season on record, the Northeast its second quietest and the North its fourth quietest. In the same months the Manaus region burned 2.87 times its typical amount, its third most intense season. The national anomaly map (Fig. 9) shows the pattern: blue across the Cerrado and the south, red around Manaus and in parts of the Northeast. Over 26 years the two series move independently (Fig. 10); in 2015, 2023 and 2026 Manaus was far above normal while Brazil was close to or below it.

Table 6. August–October 2026 by area, against the typical year (median 2003–2025)

Most intense: year with the most fire from January to October. Test error: MODIS → Suomi NPP hand-off recalibrated for that area, held-out years 2013–2025. Regions are approximate.

Fig. 8. August to October 2026 as a multiple of the typical year, by macro-region, with the rank among the 26 seasons since 2001

Fig. 9. 2026 against normal across Brazil, as shown in the application. Blue: below the typical year; red: above it. Squares of 0.5° (about 55 km).

Fig. 10. August–October fire as a multiple of the typical year, Brazil and the Manaus region, 2001–2026

Agreement with independent evidence

None of the sources in Table 7 were used to build the harmonized record, so their agreement with it is evidence that the record reflects real events.

Table 7. Agreement with independent evidence

The web application

The results are delivered as a single self-contained web page of about 12 MB that embeds all central Amazon detections and the compressed national grid. It needs no server, works offline and on phones, and is available in English and Portuguese with light and dark themes (Fig. 11). The browser engine reimplements the Python method and reproduces its monthly results exactly, so every number can be checked against the open code.

A user chooses an area around Manaus or anywhere in Brazil in four ways: a preset (Brazil, the five macro-regions, Southern Amazonas and BR-319, Pantanal, Manaus region), a click on the map, a rectangle drawn on the map, or a typed latitude and longitude. For that area the application shows the 2026 rank, the most intense year, the typical peak month, the raw detections of each satellite in 2026, the first half of November against previous years, a monthly calendar from 2001 to 2026, the held-out test error and a CSV download. The map can be switched between a street map and a satellite base map, and a ranked list marks the places where fire repeats most. A monthly bar chart below the map works as the month selector, and a month player animates the year.

Fig. 11. The Brazil section of the application with the North region selected: where fire returns (left) and the facts, monthly calendar and test error recomputed for that area (right)

Intended users

The tool is designed for five groups. Early warning teams and civil defense get a start date for preparation and a live comparison of the current season with the past, to time decrees, campaigns and burn bans. Firefighters and brigades get the peak weeks and the worst days. Land managers and enforcement agencies get the places where fire returns every year and a consistent measure of fire during bans. Health services get advance notice of the September–October smoke peak. Scientists and journalists get a 26-year harmonized series with measured error, open code and CSV downloads.

Accessibility and usability

Every color scale runs from light to dark with steadily falling lightness (94 to 32 on the OKLab scale), so it reads correctly in grayscale. In simulations of the three types of color blindness, neighbouring steps remain distinguishable (smallest difference ΔE 7.2 for deuteranopia, 8.5 for protanopia and 7.6 for tritanopia), and above and below normal use blue and red rather than red and green. All controls are buttons or form fields with visible focus, a skip link leads to the map, arrow keys move between months, and each month button announces its month and number of detections to screen readers. The animation slows down for users who turned on reduced motion. Results are written as sentences, and each area shows its own test error so users know how far to trust it.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS C6.1, VIIRS 375 m Suomi NPP and NOAA-20) and NASA Worldview imagery.
  • Processing and validation: Python 3 with pandas and NumPy.
  • Web application: JavaScript, HTML Canvas and SVG, with no frameworks and no server. The browser engine reproduces the Python results exactly.
  • 3D map: our own projection on HTML Canvas.
  • Documents and figures: LaTeX and matplotlib.
  • Hardware: personal laptops only.

How it is creative

  • It treats the end of Suomi NPP as part of the problem and keeps the record going with NOAA-20, tested on held-out years.
  • Every number comes with its own error: when a user draws an area, the browser recalibrates the hand-offs for that area and shows how well they performed.
  • It shows that the calendar must be local: the same method that ranks 2026 as Brazil's calmest season ranks it as one of the worst for Manaus.
  • The whole app is one web page with no server, so it works offline and on phones, which matters in the Amazon.

Limitations

Active fire detections mark fire burning at the moment of a satellite pass; they are not burned area and do not measure smoke. Clouds and thick smoke can hide fires, and satellites pass only a few times a day. Around Manaus, months before August 2002 rely on Terra alone and remain uncertain. Ratios are calibrated per area; in extreme drought years fires are larger and harmonized MODIS years may be slightly overestimated. The macro-regions and ready-made areas of the Brazil map are built from 55 km squares and are not official borders. Finally, a satellite cannot tell whether a fire was authorized: detections during the ban are evidence of burning, not proof of a crime, and the decree includes exceptions.

Conclusion

Harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS with month-by-month ratios turns the fragmented NASA FIRMS record into a 26-year series whose MODIS and NOAA-20 hand-offs err by 2–8% on years the model never saw, and that remains usable after the end of Suomi NPP. For Manaus the record dates the burning season, places 2026 as its third most intense season and shows that fire returns to the same places south of the rivers. For Brazil it shows the opposite picture: 2026 was the calmest season on record. A burn calendar is therefore useful only when it is computed for the place where decisions are made. Next steps are official state and municipal borders, daily updates from the FIRMS API with alerts when the season starts early, NOAA-21 as a second continuity stream, and links to air quality sensors and river levels to forecast smoke days.

Data and code availability. Application: https://clei21.github.io/amazon-fire/. Code and data: https://github.com/Clei21/amazon-fire. Full article (15 pages): https://clei21.github.io/amazon-fire/docs/AmazonFire_Article.pdf. All detections are NASA open data. This project uses NASA open data but is not an official NASA product.

Statement on the use of artificial intelligence. During this work the team used Claude (Anthropic) and ChatGPT (OpenAI) as assistants. They helped write and review the code of the application and of the data processing, produce the charts, and draft and revise the texts, including spelling and grammar. The choice of the problem, the decisions about the method and about what goes into the system, the review of the code and the checking of every number against the data were done by the team, which takes responsibility for the content and the conclusions.
